title: HE LAUGHED AT GOD’S PROMISE. THE NEXT DAY, HE WATCHED IT COME TRUE—AND DIED BEFORE HE COULD ENJOY IT.
paragraphs: HE LAUGHED AT GOD’S PROMISE. THE NEXT DAY, HE WATCHED IT COME TRUE—AND DIED BEFORE HE COULD ENJOY IT.

He was close enough to see the miracle. Close enough to touch the blessing. But the very doorway where God's promise was fulfilled became the place where his life ended. And the terrifying question is this: Can you be surrounded by God's goodness and still miss what matters most?
“And so it happened to him, for the people trampled him in the gate, and he died.” — 2 Kings 7:20 (NKJV)
Imagine starving for so long that even the memory of a full stomach feels like a cruel joke.
Imagine watching mothers weep because they cannot feed their children. Imagine an entire city trapped behind walls, slowly dying, while the enemy waits outside.
Then imagine a prophet standing in the middle of that nightmare and announcing that by tomorrow, food will be plentiful again.
Not next year.
Not after negotiations.
Not when the enemy decides to show mercy.
Tomorrow.
And somewhere in that desperate crowd, a powerful man hears the promise of God and responds with contempt.
He does not fall to his knees.
He does not ask how God will accomplish it.
He mocks the very possibility.
And before the next day is over, he will learn something that every human being needs to understand.
You can live long enough to discover that God was telling the truth—and still lose the opportunity you thought you would always have.
But this story is not simply about a man who doubted.
It is about a city that had run out of hope, four desperate outcasts who stumbled into astonishing provision, and a God who remained faithful when the circumstances made His promise seem impossible.
And somewhere in this ancient story, there may be a warning, a wound, or an invitation that reaches directly into your life today.
Because some of us have been standing at the doorway of God's truth for years.
We know the verses.
We hear the sermons.
We recognize the name of Jesus.
But knowing that God can save is not the same as surrendering to the Savior.
And that difference matters more than we sometimes realize.
The city was Samaria.
The enemy was Syria, also called Aram.
And the suffering had become almost unimaginable.

Second Kings 6 describes a siege so severe that ordinary food had become extraordinarily expensive. A donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver. Even a small quantity of material identified in the text as dove's dung commanded a price.
Then the narrative takes an even darker turn.
Two mothers make a horrifying agreement born of desperation. One child is killed and eaten, and when the second mother refuses to surrender her own child, the first appeals to the king.
It is one of the most disturbing scenes in the Old Testament.
The Bible does not celebrate it.
It exposes how far human suffering and moral collapse had gone.
The king tears his clothes.
The people are starving.
The city is breaking.
And the prophet Elisha is standing in a place where hope seems almost unreasonable.
Have you ever been there?
Not necessarily behind the walls of a besieged city.
Maybe behind the walls of a hospital room.
Maybe staring at a bank account that cannot cover another bill.
Maybe sitting in a marriage where conversations have become silence.
Maybe lying awake at three in the morning, wondering whether the person you used to be will ever return.
There are moments when suffering becomes so familiar that hope itself begins to feel offensive.
Someone says, "God is faithful."
And something inside you whispers, "Then why am I still here?"
Someone says, "Keep praying."
And you think, "Do you know how long I have already prayed?"
Someone says, "The Lord can make a way."
And your exhausted heart answers, "I have heard that before."
There is a difference between bringing wounded questions to God and deciding that His word deserves our contempt.
Scripture makes room for the first.
The Psalms are full of cries, tears, confusion, and painful questions.
But the second can slowly harden a human heart.
And that is where the officer in Samaria enters the story.
Elisha announces:

“Hear ye the word of the LORD; Thus saith the LORD, To morrow about this time shall a measure of fine flour be sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria.” — 2 Kings 7:1 (KJV)
Think about the audacity of that announcement.
A city where food had become nearly unobtainable would experience such an extraordinary reversal that flour and barley would be sold at prices radically lower than those produced by the siege.
And it would happen within approximately twenty-four hours.
There was no visible army coming to rescue them.
No announced peace treaty.
No evidence that the Syrian camp was preparing to retreat.
Only the word of the LORD.
In Hebrew, the expression is:
דְּבַר־יְהוָה — devar-YHWH
The word of the LORD.
Elisha was not offering positive thinking.
He was not selling optimism to desperate people.
He was announcing what he presented as God's own word.
And that distinction changes everything.
Biblical faith is not the power of pretending that circumstances are better than they are.
It is trusting the God who speaks truth even when circumstances appear to contradict His promise.
Then the officer speaks.
He is not an ordinary bystander. Second Kings 7:2 describes him as the officer upon whose hand the king leaned—a man of recognized position and proximity to royal power.
He has influence.
He has access.
He has probably seen enough of the kingdom's suffering to consider himself a realist.
And he answers the prophet:
“Behold, if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?” — 2 Kings 7:2 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the central expression is:
אֲרֻבּוֹת בַּשָּׁמַיִם — arubbot bashamayim
Windows, or openings, in the heavens.
He is effectively saying that even if the LORD opened heaven itself, how could such a thing happen?
The wording is important.
The officer does not merely ask for clarification.
In the narrative, his response challenges the credibility of the divine announcement.
And Elisha gives him a reply that should make every reader pay attention.
“Behold, thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof.” — 2 Kings 7:2 (KJV)
Read that again.
You will see it.
But you will not eat it.
You will witness the provision.
But you will not participate in its enjoyment.
The prophecy is not that God will fail to provide.
It is that God's provision will come exactly as announced, while this particular man will not live to benefit from it.
There is something deeply sobering about that distinction.
Because it is possible to be near the activity of God without having a heart that trusts Him.
It is possible to hear truth without receiving it.
It is possible to stand among people who are being helped and remain personally unmoved by the God who helps them.
But we must be careful here.
This passage does not teach that every struggling believer who experiences doubt will be punished with death.
It does not teach that one fearful question automatically disqualifies someone from grace.
And it certainly does not authorize anyone to tell a suffering Christian that their hardship exists because they lacked sufficient faith.
That would distort both the passage and the wider witness of Scripture.
The officer's fate is a specific prophetic judgment within a particular historical narrative.
Still, his story raises a question that should disturb our complacency.
What happens when we become so confident in our own assessment of reality that we refuse to listen to God?
Meanwhile, outside the city gate, four men are facing a different kind of crisis.
They have leprosy—or a skin condition classified under the biblical terminology often translated as leprosy—and they are living at the entrance of the city.
They are marginalized.
Hungry.
Excluded from ordinary community life.
They have no powerful position to protect.
No royal authority.
No reason to believe that the world will suddenly become kind to them.
And yet these four men make a decision that changes the entire story.
They ask one another:
“Why sit we here until we die?” — 2 Kings 7:3 (KJV)
There is something unforgettable about that question.
Why sit here until we die?
If they enter the city, there is famine.
If they remain where they are, there is no food.
If they approach the enemy camp, they may be killed.
But perhaps they will be spared.
They do not know what will happen.
They do not possess a secret revelation explaining God's plan.
They are simply desperate enough to move.
And sometimes that is where a remarkable discovery begins.
Not because human desperation forces God to act.
Not because our courage purchases a miracle.
But because God's work is often already unfolding in ways we cannot see.
The four men rise at twilight and approach the Syrian camp.
They expect soldiers.
They expect danger.
They may expect death.
Instead, they find something astonishing.
Silence.
Abandoned tents.
Horses and donkeys left behind.
Food.
Silver.
Gold.
Clothing.
An entire military camp deserted.
What happened?
Second Kings 7:6 explains that the LORD caused the Syrian army to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army.
The Syrians believed that Israel had hired powerful foreign kings to attack them.
In terror, they fled.
They abandoned their tents, animals, and supplies.
They ran for their lives.
And the most astonishing detail is this:
The LORD had already acted before the four men arrived.
The outcasts did not defeat the army.
They did not negotiate a surrender.
They did not manufacture the provision.
They discovered what God had already accomplished.
Imagine being one of those four men.
Yesterday, you were starving.
Today, you are standing before more food than you could have imagined.
Yesterday, nobody wanted you near them.
Today, you are among the first people to discover the answer to an entire city's suffering.
Yesterday, you had almost nothing.
Today, the enemy's abandoned possessions are lying before you.
The text tells us they entered a tent, ate and drank, and carried away silver, gold, and clothing.
Then they hid what they had taken.
They entered another tent and did the same.
For a moment, survival became their only concern.
And who could fail to understand their relief?
When you have been deprived for so long, abundance can feel almost unreal.
But then their consciences awaken.
They look at what they have discovered.
They remember the starving city.
And they say something extraordinary:
“We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.” — 2 Kings 7:9 (KJV)
This day is a day of good tidings.
And we are keeping silent.
In Hebrew, the phrase is:
יוֹם־בְּשֹׂרָה הוּא — yom-besorah hu
It is a day of good news.
The Hebrew noun besorah refers to news or tidings, often favorable news.
It is not identical in every historical setting to the full New Testament proclamation of Jesus Christ, but the connection is deeply meaningful.
God had provided deliverance.
The men had discovered it.
And now they understood that good news should not remain hidden while others were perishing.
They return to the city and tell the gatekeepers what they have found.
Eventually, the report reaches the king.
At first, the king is suspicious.
He thinks the Syrians may be setting a trap.
And in one sense, his caution is understandable. The city has suffered terribly, and an apparently deserted enemy camp sounds almost too good to be true.
But scouts are sent.
They discover evidence of the Syrians' retreat, including discarded garments and equipment along the road.
The report is confirmed.
The enemy is gone.
The provision is real.
And suddenly, the starving city begins to move.
Can you imagine the sound?
Doors opening.
Footsteps rushing.
People shouting.
Parents calling their children.
Neighbors repeating the news.
Food.
There is food.
The camp is empty.
The siege is broken.
What seemed impossible yesterday has become reality today.
And the market prices change just as Elisha announced.
Second Kings 7:16 records that a measure of fine flour sold for a shekel and two measures of barley for a shekel.
According to the word of the LORD.
Not according to the officer's prediction.
Not according to the military strength of Samaria.
Not according to what seemed economically or politically plausible the day before.
According to the word of the LORD.
And now the story returns to the man who mocked the promise.
The king has placed him in charge of the gate.
Think about that.
The very place where the provision would be received becomes the place of his final appointment.
He is standing where the people are rushing out.
He can see the evidence.
The abandoned camp.
The returning crowds.
The supplies being brought into the city.
Everything the prophet announced is unfolding.
The man who said it could not happen is watching it happen.
And then comes the devastating fulfillment.
“And the people trode upon him in the gate, and he died, as the man of God had said.” — 2 Kings 7:17 (KJV)
The Hebrew verb used in the account is related to רמס — ramas, meaning to trample or tread down.
The text does not describe an invisible force striking him dead.
It reports that the people trampled him at the gate.
The narrative does not explain every physical detail of the incident, but it explicitly connects his death to the prophecy spoken by Elisha.
He saw the provision.
But he did not eat it.
And verses 18–20 deliberately repeat the earlier prophecy and its fulfillment, leaving no doubt about the narrator's central point.
The word of the LORD stood.
The officer's scoffing did not overturn it.
And the man who had publicly dismissed the promise did not live to enjoy its fulfillment.
Now here is where we need to stop looking only at that officer and begin examining our own hearts.
Because not every form of unbelief sounds like open mockery.
Sometimes it sounds sophisticated.
"I believe in God, but I do not take all that repentance stuff seriously."
Sometimes it sounds comfortable.
"I know what the Bible says, but I am happy with my life."
Sometimes it sounds religious.
"I have been in church for years. Surely that is enough."
Sometimes it sounds wounded.
"I used to believe God cared, but I cannot bring myself to trust Him anymore."
And sometimes it sounds like the quiet voice of a person who has been pretending for so long that pretending has become second nature.
You know how to smile in church.
You know when to say amen.
You know the songs.
You know the familiar verses.
But when the service ends and the room becomes quiet, there are things in your life you would rather never bring into the light.
The secret bitterness.
The addiction you keep excusing.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from obedience.
The dishonesty nobody has discovered.
The prayerlessness you cover with Christian activity.
The pride that refuses correction.
The resentment you have allowed to become your identity.
And perhaps the most frightening sentence of all:
"I will deal with it later."
Later, when life settles down.
Later, when I am older.
Later, when I have enjoyed what I want to enjoy.
Later, when following Jesus becomes more convenient.
But Scripture never promises that we own tomorrow.
James 4:14 reminds us that human life is like a vapor that appears for a little while and then vanishes.
That is not a reason to live in constant panic.
It is a reason to stop treating repentance as an appointment we can endlessly postpone.
The officer in Samaria was not told that he had decades remaining to reconsider his words.
He was told that the promise would be fulfilled tomorrow.
And tomorrow came.
That is what makes this story so unsettling.
Not merely that a man died.
Every human life eventually ends.
It is that he stood so near an extraordinary demonstration of God's faithfulness, yet his final experience was the fulfillment of a warning he had refused to take seriously.
And still, we must not turn his death into a claim the Bible does not make.
Second Kings 7 does not tell us the eternal destiny of this officer.
It does not reveal the complete condition of his soul at death.
It does not permit us to declare with certainty where he went after dying.
The passage tells us what happened in Samaria.
And that is serious enough.
But there is another man in Scripture whose story helps us understand the Gospel more fully.
A man who also stood close to death.
A man who also had no guarantee of another tomorrow.
A man who had done wrong and could no longer pretend otherwise.
He was hanging on a cross beside Jesus.
One of the criminals crucified with Christ joined in mocking Him.
But the other rebuked his companion, acknowledged that they were receiving the consequences of their deeds, and declared that Jesus had done nothing wrong.
Then he turned to Christ and said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42 (KJV)
There was no time left for him to rebuild his reputation.
No opportunity to spend years proving his sincerity.
No chance to repay the people he had wronged.
He could not climb down from the cross and begin a new religious career.
He had nothing to offer Jesus except the confession of a guilty man and a plea for mercy.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43 (KJV)
Do you see the breathtaking contrast?
In Samaria, a powerful officer rejected a promise and saw its fulfillment without enjoying its provision.
At Calvary, a condemned criminal turned to Jesus and received a promise of paradise.
The two narratives are not identical, and Scripture does not present them as a formal pair.
But read together, they remind us that human status cannot secure our future and human failure need not place us beyond the mercy of Christ.
The officer had royal access.
The criminal had no earthly power.
The officer stood at a gate where provision was arriving.
The criminal hung beside the Savior who gives eternal life.
And the criminal's hope was not in his own worthiness.
It was in Jesus.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sinners become acceptable to God by pretending they have never sinned.
Not that we can purchase forgiveness through religious activity.
Not that we earn salvation by becoming impressive enough for heaven.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again.
Paul summarizes the message in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures.
The Greek word often translated as grace is:
χάρις — charis
Grace.
God's undeserved favor.
And Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
The Greek text begins:
Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως
Te gar chariti este sesosmenoi dia pisteos.
For by grace you have been saved through faith.
Notice where salvation begins.
Not with your ability to impress God.
Not with the number of people who admire your spirituality.
Not with the amount of money you can give.
Not with the perfection of your past.
With grace.
And grace is not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
The same Christ who forgives also calls us to repentance and a transformed life.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia refers to repentance, a turning of mind and heart that involves a changed response to God.
Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people feel temporarily better.
He came to save sinners.
To reconcile us to God.
To break the dominion of sin.
To make us new.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior has never been merely about scandal.
It is about what Jesus does with people whose stories seem beyond repair.
Think of Peter.
He denied knowing Jesus three times.
Think of the tears after the rooster crowed.
The shame.
The memory of his own words.
The awful realization that he had failed the Lord he claimed he would never abandon.
And yet, after the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with responsibility to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Think of Saul.
A persecutor of the church.
A man who approved of violence against believers.
Yet the risen Christ confronted him, and the man who once tried to destroy the faith became an apostle who proclaimed Jesus.
Think of the Samaritan woman in John 4.
Jesus knew the painful and complicated truth of her life.
He did not need to be deceived about her past in order to speak to her about living water.
She left her water jar and went to tell others about Him.
Different lives.
Different wounds.
Different failures.
One Savior whose mercy is greater than the reputation people thought would define them forever.
And maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be remembered for your worst moment.
Maybe someone still introduces you through a mistake you made years ago.
Maybe your family knows the scandal but has never seen the private repentance.
Maybe you have been carrying shame so long that you cannot imagine a life without it.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not need to pretend your sin was harmless in order to forgive it.
He does not need to rewrite history by calling evil good.
He rewrites the future of those who come to Him by grace.
The cross tells the truth about sin's seriousness.
The resurrection announces the victory of Christ.
And the Gospel invites sinners to stop hiding and come into the light.
You may not be able to change yesterday.
But by God's grace, yesterday does not have to remain the master of your tomorrow.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
It does not mean broken trust is restored instantly.
It does not mean every relationship will return to what it once was.
But it does mean forgiveness is real.
Redemption is real.
And the transforming power of Jesus Christ is not a religious slogan.
It is the hope at the heart of the Christian faith.
Now return with me, just for a moment, to those four men outside Samaria.
They found food while an entire city was starving.
They could have hidden everything and thought only of themselves.
But eventually they said:
"This is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace."
What a searching picture of responsibility.
They had received good news.
Others needed to hear it.
And silence was no longer something they could comfortably justify.
Christian, what have you done with the good news entrusted to you?
Not the news that your life is perfect.
Not the claim that every prayer will be answered exactly as you desire.
Not a promise that following Jesus guarantees wealth, health, or an easy road.
The real good news.
That Christ died for sinners.
That He rose from the dead.
That forgiveness is offered through Him.
That repentance and faith are not reserved for people with spotless histories.
That the weary can come to Him.
That the ashamed do not need to hide forever.
That the lost can be found.
That the dead in sin can be made alive in Christ.
Someone in your family needs to hear that.
Someone who used to attend church but has quietly disappeared.
Someone who is smiling publicly and unraveling privately.
Someone who has convinced themselves that God would never receive them again.
Someone who thinks Christianity is only for people who have never made a mess of their lives.
Someone who has never opened a Bible but desperately wants to know whether forgiveness is possible.
Maybe sharing this article will not change their life immediately.
Maybe they will read only a paragraph.
But maybe one sentence will make them stop.
Maybe they will remember a Scripture they heard as a child.
Maybe they will open the Bible for themselves.
Maybe they will pray honestly for the first time in years.
We cannot manufacture another person's conversion.
Only God can bring spiritual life.
But we can faithfully bear witness.
Not as a performance of spirituality, and not to prove anything to anyone, but because the Gospel is too precious to be treated as a private possession.
Send it quietly to a friend who needs hope.
Let the message travel farther than your own circle.
And if you have made it this far, I want to ask you something more personal.
Where are you in this story?
Are you like the officer, so convinced that nothing can change that you have stopped taking God's word seriously?
Are you like the four men, exhausted and desperate, wondering whether there is any reason to take another step?
Are you like the starving city, waiting for relief and struggling to imagine how it could come?
Or are you like the criminal beside Jesus, finally recognizing that you cannot save yourself and asking the Savior for mercy?
You do not have to pretend in order to answer.
You do not have to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
You do not have to reveal details that should remain private.
Your testimony may encourage someone who thinks their story is already over.
Let this be more than another article people read and forget.
Let it become a conversation where believers encourage one another, pray for one another, and point one another back to the truth of Scripture.
Not because saving a post earns favor with God.
Save it as a reminder to open 2 Kings 6–7 and read the complete account for yourself.
Because the deepest nourishment will never come merely from reading what someone says about the Bible.
It comes from returning to the Word itself.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to produce emotional stories.
Not simply to gain views, reactions, or followers.
But to help people encounter biblical truth, examine their lives honestly, grow in their understanding of Scripture, and follow Jesus Christ with greater faithfulness.
And if this ministry has helped you, I want to invite you into something deeper than an occasional encounter with an article on your feed.
Invite your family, your Christian friends, those who have drifted from church, and even those who are still exploring what it means to believe in Jesus.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond a moment of inspiration into a life of learning, prayer, repentance, obedience, and spiritual maturity.
And for those who believe in this mission and are financially able, there is another way to stand with us.
For some, this may be a meaningful part of their regular Christian giving.
It does not purchase His blessing.
It does not replace your responsibility to support your local church or other obligations you have prayerfully made.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing and sincere.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
The same passage teaches that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion.
Not through fear.
Not through guilt.
Not by suggesting that God's favor can be purchased.
But through shared conviction that making biblical teaching and discipleship resources available to more people is a worthwhile mission.
These products are simply another way to encourage faith, share a biblical message, or give someone a meaningful gift. They are not measures of spiritual maturity.
And the free Gospel resources remain central to our desire to serve.
Because the purpose is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to point people to Jesus.
And that brings us back to the gate of Samaria.
I cannot stop thinking about that man.
He heard the prophet.
He mocked the promise.
He saw the provision.
And he died before he could enjoy it.
There is something deeply tragic about seeing a promise fulfilled and realizing that the opportunity to enjoy its provision has passed.
But there is also something wonderfully hopeful about the four desperate men who found the abandoned camp.
They did not create the deliverance.
They discovered it.
Then they carried the news to others.
And there is something even greater about the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
We did not defeat sin and death by our own power.
Christ accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
We do not come to Him carrying enough good works to pay for salvation.
We come with empty hands, trusting His finished work.
And we do not need to wait until we become impressive, respectable, or publicly admired before calling on His name.
The invitation is for sinners.
For the proud who need to humble themselves.
For the wounded who need hope.
For the religious who have confused familiarity with surrender.
For the ashamed who believe they have gone too far.
For the exhausted who are barely holding on.
For the person reading this who has not prayed sincerely in years.
Jesus says in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
What a promise.
Not a promise that life will suddenly become painless.
Not a guarantee that every earthly situation will change tomorrow.
But a declaration from the Savior that those who come to Him will not be cast out.
So come.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come with the truth about your sin.
Come with your unanswered questions.
Come with your broken history.
Come trusting Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, rather than your own ability to make yourself worthy.
If you do not know what to pray, you can begin simply:

"Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to turn from sin and follow You. I place my trust in You, not in my own goodness. Amen."
Those words are not a magic formula.
Salvation is not produced by reciting a particular prayer.
The invitation of the Gospel is to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
And if you already belong to Him but have wandered, return.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Ask for help where you have become trapped.
Reconnect with a faithful local church.
Open the Scriptures again.
Do not let shame persuade you to stay away from the very Savior whose mercy you need.
And do not let familiarity with holy things replace a living relationship with the Holy One.
The officer in Samaria could not stop God's word from coming true.
But the deeper lesson for us is not that every doubter should expect his fate.
It is that God's truth deserves to be taken seriously, and our lives are too brief to build them on the illusion that we will always have another tomorrow.
If the Lord were to call me to account for my life today, would I be resting in Jesus Christ—or merely in the fact that I have heard about Him?
That question is not meant to drive you into despair.
It is meant to direct you to the Savior.
Because the Gospel does not end at the gate where a man was trampled.
It leads us to the cross where the Son of God gave His life for sinners.
And beyond the cross stands an empty tomb.
The risen Christ is our hope.
The mercy of God is not a rumor.
Forgiveness is not a fantasy.
And the invitation to come to Jesus is not something you have to earn.
But above all, do not leave this story merely impressed by a miracle.
Leave it looking to Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy is not failing to receive something we wanted in this life.
It is spending our lives near the truth about the Savior without ever turning to Him in faith.
Do not wait until the final page of your life to discover that the grace you kept postponing was the very grace you needed all along.
